items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I seek leave to move without
notice or debate a motion congratulating th e Speaker on his performance in the New
York City Marathon.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for such a course  of action. Is there any objection?
There appears to be none. Thank you all very, very much.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD

Insurance—Proposal for State-owned Company
1. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister of Finance:
Does he stand by his statement that a publicly-owned insurer is a “dumb idea”?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: The Minister stands by all his statements that he has made about the idea of
a taxpayer-owned insurer. In addition to calling it dumb, he also said the idea was stupid
and crazy. Furthermore, he stands by anot her part of his statement in the House
yesterday, which was: “A billion-dollar impost on New Zealand taxpayers arises exactly
from financial institutions taking too much  risk and loading it on to the Government.
That is why his proposition is stupid.” He pa rticularly stands by this other part of his
statement: “we want to avoid the taxpayer having to take th e kinds of risks that have
destroyed public finances in other devel oped countries. That is why the Government
taking on even more insurance risk than it currently holds is crazy.”

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is he calling Ross Armstrong, the former president of the
National Party, dumb for supporting a publicly owned insurer like KiwiAssure?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Are you referring to the form er Labour Party first mover,
Ross Armstrong? That is right. Look, I have been here for 5 years now but I must admit
that I have not actually met Ross. Possibly the Minister of Finance has, but I suspect he
is not actually getting the advice from Ross Armstrong at this point in time.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is he calling the 850,000 cust omers of Kiwibank, the vast
majority of whom would like to have a New Zealand-owned insurer—is he calling those
hundreds of thousands of New Zealanders dumb?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I cannot put words in the mouth of the Minister of Finance,
but on behalf of the Minister of Finance I say that what I think he is calling dumb is the
idea that you would want to take on a whole lot more risk on behalf of taxpayers.
Private sector insurers are paying out $20 billion as a re sult of the Christchurch
14392 Questions for Oral Answer 6 Nov 2013
earthquakes, and the only question is how mu ch of that $20 billion would Mr Parker
like the taxpayers to take on.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Was it a dumb idea for John Key to say that he was considering
an investment by the Crown in Chorus on the same day Steven Joyce and the Minister
of Finance were saying that investments like that would be a radical shift into a State-
controlled economy reminiscent of the 1970s?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Generally, when the Opposition fires out a gag that misfires
because it is incorrect and the quote is wrong, it does not come back for another smack
the next day. The reality is the Prime Minister  did not say that. He just did not rule out
options and you are the ones—the Opposition— who are trying to put words in his
mouth.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is he calling Adam Hamilton, Sid Holland, Keith
Holyoake, John Marshall, and Robert Muldoo n—the last four being former National
Prime Ministers—dumb for supporting a State-owned insurer?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The difficulty for the member is that we are 40 years on
from the last of those Prime Ministers. I appr eciate that the member is not, but the rest
of the world is, and in a modern, open ec onomy where New Zealand does well, more
State-controlled influence in the econom y would only damage the New Zealand
economy at a time when it is performing very well relative to the rest of the developed
world and, frankly, performing better every month.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is he calling the editors of the Press, the Southland Times, the
Dominion Post , and many others who have written editorials supportive of Labour’s
KiwiAssure dumb?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I must have read a different paper. I read the Dominion
Post and also the New Zealand Herald , which is the one that the member forgot to
mention. I think the New Zealand Herald comment, and I am not quoting verbatim, said
something like “Let us hope this thing is forgotten as quickly as it has been thought up.”
The Dominion Post sat there and said “Oh, we don’t know about this—sounds risky.”,
or words to that effect. The r eality of this half-f ormed, half-baked proposal is that all it
would do is create significant additional fiscal risk for Ne w Zealand taxpayers at the
very time when the world has worked out that  that sort of fiscal risk can be highly
damaging to economies, to families, and to any people in a country.

items.speaker: Rt Hon John Key
items.text: Not only has he seen any repor ts on establishing, potentially, a
new State-owned insurance company but also  has the Minister of  Finance seen any
reports on what was the last political part y to actually sell a State-owned insurance
company?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Minister of Finance will have no responsibility for that.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Point of order, the Hon Gerry—[Interruption] Order! This is a point
of order. It is entitled to be heard and will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: We had an interesting ruling yesterday that suggested that the
Prime Minister could not be as ked a question that related to advice from officials if that
advice related to a privately owned company. I th ink that is a ruling that will need to be
looked at in the future, but what  would appear to have happen ed here is that we have a
question from the Opposition asking whether or not the Minister agrees with its
proposition that it is a good idea to set up a State-owned insurer. He is now simply
being asked the question in reverse, which is  whether there has been  an incidence of a
Government selling a State-owned insurer. That surely cannot be out of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate the poin t the Minister is maki ng. I had a look at the
Hansard yesterday. As the Deputy Speaker found yesterday, the Speaker needs to
quickly ascertain whether he thinks it is within the responsibility of the Minister to
6 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14393
whom the question is asked. I have determined that it is not. I ha ve ruled the question
out of order and that is the end of the matter.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: In reaching—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I certainly want to hear the supplementary question.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: In reaching his conclusion that a State-owned insurer being
established by any future Government would be a dumb idea, did he consider any past
actions by a Government relating to the sale of a State-owned insurer?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, of course you would do that, and the Minister of
Finance has. Of course, there was a time in the past when we had a State-owned insurer
and it was, of course, sold by a Government—

items.speaker: Rt Hon John Key
items.text: Really?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes. In 1990, actually, it was sold by a Government. In
fact, a Labour Government so ld it at that time, which makes it slightly weird that
Labour is asking to create another one now, but that is entirely consistent with its “yeah,
nah, yeah” approach—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have heard enough of the answer.
Irrigation Projects—Treasury Analysis
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements regarding Government policy?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that “The Government supports
irrigation because of its poten tial for significant economic advantages.”, and how does
he reconcile that statement with advice from Treasury, which, in examining the
proposed irrigation schemes, came to the c onclusion that they generally promised poor
to average rates of return?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: With reference to his answer to my last supplementary question,
then how does he reconcile that support with the fact th at Treasury, when analysing
irrigation projects, came to the conclusion that these projects generally promised poor to
average rates of return?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have not seen the specific advice—that would have been sent
to other Ministers—but what I can say is th at there have certainly been projects where
irrigation schemes have made a significant economic difference to New Zealand. As we
know with the South Island, probably one of the fastest ways, actually, to lift economic
growth in the South Island would be to ensu re that there is irrigation. A huge amount of
water that falls on the South Island from snow or rain basically pours out to sea, and if
that was stored it would allow for greater de velopment of the South Island, as would be
true in parts of the East Coast of New Zealand.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How could it be economically prudent for a Government to
spend up to $400 million—which is the number that has been floated—to support the
irrigation projects that are on the agenda currently when Treasury analysed the projects
and came to the conclusion that these projects  generally promised poor to average rates
of return? How could it be economically prudent to support such a project?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I said, I have not seen the specific advice, but what I can
say is that it is important to understand that  although the Government is prepared to put
in up to $400 million, it is actually as an e quity player. So, over time, there is the
expectation that cash would be returned. But if the member really wants to get into
following, and being a worshipper of, Treasury advice—and that would be a great thing
if the member decides he wants to do that—t hen he should go and ask Treasury what it
thinks of his barmy idea about power.
14394 Questions for Oral Answer 6 Nov 2013

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that Treasury came to the conclusion that “farm gate
analysis indicates that irri gating the proposed areas would (in aggregate) constitute a
loss-making investment”, how can it possi bly be economically prudent for the
Government to put hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers’ money into a loss-
making investment?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, as I say, I have not seen the specific analysis, but over a
long period of time there is no que stion, I think, that if there is greater irrigation in the
parts of New Zealand where there is a shortage of water, that will have a significant
impact not only on the GDP of New Zealand but overall on the jobs and opportunities.
That member, as we now know, is  a weekly participant on the Farmingshow. I know
that, because David Cunliffe gave it the one-finger salute and decided—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This has very little to do with the answer required.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table the Treas ury papers from the Official
Information Act request, with all the Treasury papers, for the Prime Minister’s benefit,
about irrigation.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table a volume of Treasury papers, I take it?

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action? There was objection.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: With regard to the broader economic effects that the Prime
Minister referenced in his answer to the la st question, is he aware that in Treasury’s
analysis of the broader economic effects it found that those broader economic effects
arose principally from the stimulatory eff ects of the construction activity—so it was the
construction activity alone, or principally, that produced the broader economic effects—
and if you could construct anything and produce those kinds of stimulatory effects, why
is the Prime Minister proposing to spend the money on these projects?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Maybe the answer to this ques tion lies in the valuation of a
property that has access to wate r and irrigation. If it is so lely of economic benefit to
both the farmer and the country to build an irrigation project and not actually use it, then
maybe the member would like to explain why farms that are irrigated sell for so much
more and have so much greater economic productivity. I think the member can sit there,
if he likes, and probably misrepresent Treas ury—I do not really know, I have not read
the research—but the bottom line is that Ne w Zealand would be well served if it
advances irrigation. I encour age the member to go on the Farmingshow, on which he
now has replaced David Cunliffe, and tell the farmers exactly what he thinks.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Prime Minister honestly trying to tell the House that his
approach to economic development is to iden tify things that the Prime Minister would
just like to build—because he thinks they are good things—and that regardless of the
analysis that is conducted by Treasury, whose job it is to analyse these proposals, he just
happens to like those proposals so he is go ing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars
on them?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Let me make this challenge to  the member, then. We will go
over to Treasury and we will ask, on a scale of one to 10, how much it dislikes these
things. If it dislikes irrigation more than it dislikes his power programme, we will stop
our programme. But if it dislikes his pow er programme more, will he campaign on
stopping his? I do not think so.
Economy—Business Confidence and Employment
3. Hon TAU HENARE (National) to the Minister of Finance: What reports has he
received on the economy—and especially on further signs of improving economic
momentum and increasing business and consumer confidence?
6 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14395
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance : I have received a number of reports  providing further evidence of good
momentum in the New Zeala nd economy and of improving confidence. For example,
Treasury this week issued its monthly Economic Indicators outlook for October. It said
that the positive outlook for the economy was reinforced by the latest trade data, which
confirmed that the recovery from last  summer’s drought is under way. It also
highlighted rising net migration inflows, buoyant business sentiment in the September
quarter, and other surveys reporting in creases in confidence and activity. The
Government is supporting these positive developments through its economic
programme, and especia lly through the Business Growth  Agenda, which is focused on
creating the conditions for businesses to invest, grow, and create new jobs.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What does Treasury’s monthly Economic Indicators  report say
about business confidence among New Zealand firms and their intentions to hire more
workers?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Treasury says that business confidence in the economic
outlook has risen to the highest level in many years. It pointed to the Quarterly Survey
of Business Opinion from the New Zeala nd Institute of Economic Research, which
showed that firms experienced an improvement in their own activity over the September
quarter, and that even more businesses believ ed that activity would increase further in
the December quarter. The survey reported modest employment growth, but hiring
intentions were rising strongly and are positiv e. Activity in the manufacturing sector, in
particular, continues to increase. This is supported by ongoing strong numbers in the
Performance of Manufacturing Index.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How is the higher business conf idence being reflected in other
economic indicators, especially in respect of the employment markets?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The household labour force survey and the quarterly
employment survey both came out today. They confirmed that increased business
confidence is being translat ed into more jobs and higher employment. The household
labour force survey showed that employmen t was up by 1.2 percent in the quarter. As
an annual figure that is 53,000 more people in  work, or a 2.4 percen t increase for the
year. At the same time, unemployment dr opped from 6.4 percent to 6.2 percent.
Obviously, we are very keen to see that come down further, but the trend is encouraging
and better than in many other developed c ountries around the world. It is also pleasing
that the M āori employment rate rose over the year. It is now also worth noting that the
“neets” rate—that is, young people not in education, employment, or training—fell over
the quarter from 12.1 percent to 11.4 percent, which is the lowest level since December
2008, before the global financial crisis.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What do official employment statistics show about recent
movements in incomes relative to the cost of living, and how is this assisting families to
get ahead?

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Real wages are stagnant.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I know I am going to disappoint  Mr Little, who is always
talking the place down. The quarterly employme nt survey shows that average ordinary
time hourly earnings rose 2.6 percent over the year and were up from 2.1 percent in the
previous quarter. This compares with inflat ion of 1.4 percent for the year, meaning that
people in work—and there are more of them —have the conditions to make steady and
consistent gains in their incomes. Adding in a long run of low mortga ge interest rates,
these are very helpful conditions for familie s and households to get ahead. It is also
worth noting that not only are average hourly earnings up but the number of hours being
worked has increased as well. Paid hours are up by 2.7 percent over the year. These
14396 Questions for Oral Answer 6 Nov 2013
improving figures flow from careful Governme nt policies that suppor t growth and jobs
being translated into real-world situations for New Zealand families.
Broadband, Ultra-fast—Infrastructure Pricing and Contract with Chorus
4. Hon SHANE JONES (Labour) to the Prime Minister: Does he have confidence
in his Ministers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Has he advised Minister Joyce to  inform Chorus that it has taken
its own financial risk, and parking up divi dends to its owners and managing its own
debt is a better opti on than fabricating to the market a possible insolvency, thus hoping
to get corporate welfare from the Minister for Economic Development?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not aware of any conversat ions that Minister Joyce has
had with Chorus. In fact, I am now very recently advised that he has not had any
conversations with Chorus. But what I can sa y for the benefit of the member, if he is
interested, is that the Government is now assessing the situation. It is not a matter of
whether there is corporate welfare or othe rwise. The Government is committed to the
long-term build of ultra-fast broadband, and in the course of time the Government will
assess all of the options available to it and decide what the next course of action is.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Why is he, his former Minister  Steven Joyce, and his current
Minister for Communications and Information Technology, Amy Adams, so surprised
at the Commerce Commission’s decision to dr op the copper price given that Steven
Joyce’s 2011 telecommunications company legislation clearly stated that there would be
a 3-year moratorium before the move to a cost-plus model for wholesale copper pricing,
which the Commerce Commission is now implementing, and that Chorus’ first
prospectus clearly stated this as a risk, as  did the regulatory impact statement for the
Government’s only 2011 law?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Gosh, the member is a long way back these days.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Point of order—[ Interruption] Order!
This is a point of order and it will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That was a very direct
question about policy. You ruled the Prime Mini ster out of order in an earlier answer
today, and he has now repeated the very thi ng you had ruled him out of order for in an
answer that followed. I ask you to make sure  that the Prime Minister adheres to the
Standing Orders.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I will certainly do my best to make sure that the Prime Minister
adheres to the Standing Orders. His start of  the answer was unsatisfactory. I told the
Prime Minister so. The question has now been asked and I invite the Prime Minister to
answer it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, I think it is very fair to say that no one back in 2011
actually predicted that there w ould be such a dramatic fall in  copper prices. In fact, my
understanding is that the member believed that copper prices would go up, not actually
go down. So that fall has certainly caught th e market by surprise. There were many,
many analysts who looked at the situation as a result of the legisla tion that was brought
in, and, in fact, at the contra ct that Chorus signed, and not one analyst actually noted
that there was a significant likelihood that there would be such a dramatic decrease in
the copper price.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: I seek leave to table page 204 of  Chorus’s first prospectus, which
clearly sets out its awareness of—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We do not need any more de scription. I just want to clarify
whether that document is clearly available if members want it.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: It is an old document. It is difficult to access.
6 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14397

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On the basis—[ Interruption] I think that members have the ability
to access that if they want it.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Can he assure this House that ne ither Steven Joyce nor his ministry
provided any kind of guarantee at the demerg er of Telecom that has led Chorus to
believe that its profitability would not be a dversely affected by the legislated move to
cost-plus unbundled bitstream access pricing?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My advice is that the Minister made no such assurance.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: In light of the statement by Chor us yesterday that it would “discuss
with the Crown whether Chorus was still a cr edible UFB partner in the way intended at
demerger …”, does he believe that all part ies—all parties—tendering on the ultra-fast
broadband contract did so on an equal footing; if they did not, will he sack Steven Joyce
as the Minister responsible for that debacle?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: This will come as a huge disappointment to the member, but,
no, I will not be sacking Steven Joyce an y time soon. It is very important to
understand—[Interruption]—any time soon. I am feeling good about it. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Prime Minister now has a right to answer the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What the member is clearly demonstrating is that she is not
committed to the roll-out of ultra-fast broadband. I really look forward—

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That was a very precise
question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It was not a very precise question. It was quite a long
question that included a comment around whether a Minister would retain his job or not.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: When Minister Joyce told Pa rliament: “These new broadband
networks will provide an economic step change as we leapfrog many of our competitors
…”, did he add: “We will probably need to bail out a sharemarket company and twist
the regulatory framework of the Commerce Commission.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think that, firstly, it is very important to understand that there
is no bailout taking place. The Government has a strong commitment to ultra-fast
broadband. The Government now has to look at the implications for the ultra-fast
broadband programme as a result of the Commerce Commission’s ruling. If the member
is basically telling New Zealanders that he  does not support the roll-out of ultra-fast
broadband, that is going to be a great discussion to have in 2014.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Can the Prime Minister assure this House that neither he nor “Mr
Fix-it” will—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Can I ask the member to rephrase his
question.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Can the Prime Minister and multi-millionaire former
businessman—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I now invite the member to ask a
question in line with the Standing Orders, and if he does not do so this time, we will be
moving on.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Can the Prime Minister a nd the Minister for Economic
Development assure or guarantee this House that his Government will not bail out this
share market company, but, rather, will enforc e the contract and not give in to their
protestations for corporate welfare?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What I can say is that it is hi ghly likely that the Minister of
Communications and Information Technology will have a little more to say about this
tomorrow. She is likely to be able to give  an indication of how the Government will
now try to understand fully the ruling from the Commerce Commission and the possible
alternatives and options available. But the Government is committed to ultra-fast
broadband. The interesting thing with ultra-fast broadband is that it is going to be rolled
14398 Questions for Oral Answer 6 Nov 2013
out—both through the Rural Broadb and Initiative and with fi bre—up in that member’s
part of the world, which happens to be one of the few parts of New Zealand that is
actually not going ahead economically at the ra te that the Government wants. Actually,
I just wonder whether next year  that member will be struttin g his stuff, telling the good
people of Northland that they  do not deserve ultra-fast br oadband. If they vote Labour,
they will be on old technology.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My area is not actually in the
grid that is going to get this broadband outreach.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is not even remotely accurate as a point of order.
Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting—Appointment of Sri Lanka to
Chair
5. Hon PETER DUNNE (Leader—United Future)  to the Minister of Foreign

items.speaker: Affairs
items.text: What advice has he received on the call from Amnesty International opposing
the appointment of Sri Lankan Presiden t Mahinda Rajapaksa as Chair of the
Commonwealth for the next 2 years, and hos t of next week’s Commonwealth Heads of
Government meeting?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.role: Actin g Minister of Foreign Affairs
items.text: I have
received a range of advice on the Comm onwealth Heads of Government Meeting
(CHOGM) and the issues raised by Amnesty International. The decision to accept Sri
Lanka’s offer to host and chair CHOGM  was made collectively by Commonwealth
countries in Perth in 2011. By offering to  host CHOGM, the Sri Lankan Government
knows that it is opening itself up to scrutiny on human rights and reconciliation issues.
It is the New Zealand Government’s position that the most constructive thing that New
Zealand can do is to engage and use the oppor tunity to examine progress. The Minister
of Foreign Affairs will be visiting the north  of Sri Lanka during CHOGM next week to
do precisely that.

items.speaker: Hon Peter Dunne
items.text: Has the Minister seen the various  reports of human rights abuses
occurring in Sri Lanka, and has the Govern ment sought to make any expression of
concern about those issues to the Government  of Sri Lanka in advance of next week’s
CHOGM?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The Minister receives a range of advice on
those issues. He has visited Sri Lanka twic e this year, and he does raise those very

Housing, Affordable—Options Paper and Cost of Building Materials
7. MARK MITCHELL (National—Rodney) to the Minister of Commerce: What
steps is the Government taking to intr oduce more competition into the housing
construction market?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: One of the five main contributors to
the high cost of construction in New Z ealand, as identified by the Productivity
Commission last year, is the cost of buildi ng materials, which can be as much as 30
percent higher than in Australia. That is  why the Minister of Housing and I have
released the Residential Construction Market Study—Options Paper. This paper sets out
options to introduce more competition into the housing construction sector, which can
bring down the costs of home building materials. The options include proposing
increased transparency, simplified complian ce, changes to anti-dumping duties, and
tariff concessions, which can bring down the costs of new-home building materials.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: How will these options help to increase competition and lower the
cost of building materials?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: More competition in the building construction sector can lead
to more choice and lower costs for consumer s. Submissions to the market study earlier
this year raised concerns that it was diffi cult for good quality and new products to come
into the New Zealand market. The paper out lines options that c ould be made with
changes to the regulatory fram ework and to promote competit ion to make it easier for
these quality products to come to the New Zealand market. More choice and more
competition is a win-win for all of New Zealand.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: After all the tough talk from the Minister of Hous ing, scapegoating
local councils for his failed housing policy, will the Government now be brave enough
to tackle the vested interests holding back competition in the building supplies market?

items.text: This Government certainly has the courage to deal with the
crisis of housing th at was inherited in 2008 by th is Government, where building

The suite of measures we are undert aking—freeing up land supply, Resource
Management Act reform, reining in council c ontribution rates, halving interest rates for
New Zealanders, and investing in skills a nd productivity—is the courage of conviction
to help New Zealand families address their building construction costs.

would tackle the vested interests in the building supplies market. He did not address that

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member wants to go back and look at his question, it certainly
has been adequately addressed.

point that not all victims of sexual abuse are women. In fact, young men, older men, and

Prison Facilities—Redevelopment
10. JACQUI DEAN (National—Waitaki)  to the Minister of Corrections : What
recent announcements has she made on the redevelopment of prison facilities?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I recently announced that
Auckland Prison (Maximum Security Division) is  to be completely rebuilt to provide a
more secure, safe, and modern facility. The maximum security wing is the only one of
its kind in the country and houses this c ountry’s most dangerous and most difficult
prisoners. However, it is now 45 years old a nd is becoming increasingly expensive to
maintain, and it simply does not have the capacity to deliver specialist rehabilitation and
mental health services. The wing will be designed, built, financed, and maintained
under a public-private partnership, but the Depa rtment of Corrections will continue to
manage the prison’s day-to-day operations.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What unique features will the rebu ilt maximum security wing have to
allow corrections staff to better manage prisoners?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The rebuild will improve the conditions for staff so that they
can work more effectively with prisoners to  lower their security classification. The new
building will also house a specialist mental health unit for prisone rs with severe to
moderate needs, which will provide care to  offenders who currently have to be
transferred back and forth from the Mason Clin ic. This, in turn, will  ease pressure on
the Mason Clinic for the wide r population. The facility, whic h is scheduled to open in
mid-2017, will be a world-class maximum security  unit, will put public and staff safety
first, and will allow corrections to more  effectively manage these very dangerous
prisoners.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What other upgrades has she announced to prison infrastructure?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Today I announced that $81.3 million is being invested to
upgrade another five prisons to improve their safety and security a nd to provide better
facilities for prisoner rehabil itation and training. Major in frastructure works will soon
begin at Invercargill, Wha nganui, and Tongariro prisons, with work already under way
6 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14405
at Waikeria and Rolleston prisons. Not only wi ll the investment we are making in these
five prisons improve their security but also we are making sure that they are in the best
possible position to help the G overnment achieve its target of reducing re-offending by
25 percent by 2017.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is her target to improve the safety of corrections officers by 50
percent through initiatives like this ambiti ous enough, when it is not even getting her
back to rates before she came into office, w ith serious prisoner as saults on staff having
almost doubled in the last 3 years?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I think it is a bit rich for an Opposition member from the
previous Labour Government to address a question on the issue of prisoner safety to this
Government, which has spent millions of dollars, has put in place an external advisory
group to work with staff on staff safety, and ha s put out and set a target to improve staff
safety, when the previous Labour Governme nt did absolutely nothing over 9 years to
address the concerns around staff safety.
Christchurch, Recovery—Housing Availability

items.text: How many affordable homes will be built in Christchurch, given that
Gerry Brownlee says that the Government is already well on the way to delivering more
housing in Christchurch at a scale and time line that equals Labour’s plan?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I do wish that the member would quote my colleague
accurately. He said that we ar e ahead of the curve as far as  the potential plan from the
Labour Party is concerned.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he agree with New Bright on resident Sue Davidson when she
says that they have been forgotten, and why after 3 years has the Government never
proposed anywhere in Canterbury the kind of innovative, hands-on approach that
Labour has announced for New Brighton?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Although I do not have responsibility for the
regeneration programme in the suburb of New Brighton in Christchurch, what I can tell

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: With the Ministry of Busine ss, Innovation and Employment
estimating a shortfall of 7,000 homes in Christ church, why is he refusing to get behind

evidence points to a crisis at the affordable end of the market?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: As I said earlier when answering a question as the
Minister responsible for the Earthquake  Commission, it does not  matter how many

14406 Questions for Oral Answer 6 Nov 2013
still available but a recognition that we do have to replace a good number of the nearly

World War I Centenary—Commemorations and National War Memorial Park
12. CHRIS AUCHINVOLE (National)  to the Minister for Arts, Culture and

items.speaker: Heritage
items.text: How does the Government intend to ma rk the centenary of the First World
War?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.role: Minist er for Arts, Culture and Heritage

items.text: The Government has developed a compre hensive programme called WW100 to mark
the First World War. WW100 has a very stro ng digital presence, and I know that Mr
Grant Robertson will be delighted to vi sit the website—ww100.govt.nz—because he is
a 21 st century guy, and also on Facebook and Twitter. The centrepiece will be New
Zealand Memorial Park in Wellington, wh ich will be opened on Anzac Day in 2015.
Funding has been allocated for national and local centenary projec ts. The Government
is also supporting the Auckland War Memo rial Museum’s Cenotaph database, which
will provide a page for every New Zealander who served in the First World War. There
is also an international component. Heritage tr ails in other countries  will tell the stories
of New Zealand’s involvement in battles from Gallipoli to Western Europe.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How is the National War Memorial Park progressing?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Brilliantly. The Minist er of Transport and I
recently visited the trench that will take State Highway 1 underground at the Buckle
Street part of the park. Construction is 3 days behind schedule, which is a fantastic
achievement for such a major project. It is a huge credit to Mr Brownlee, his transport
officials, and those in the New Zealand Transport Agency.
Interislander Ferries—Aratere Malfunction

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from the Rt Hon Winston Peters seeking to
debate under Standing Order 386 the state of the interisland ferry service following the
ferry Aratere suffering mechanical problems in Cook Strait last night. The Aratere’s
mechanical problem of yesterday is a pa rticular case of recen t occurrence involving
ministerial responsibility. However, Kiwi Rail’s response is ongoing. Surveyors are
ascertaining the damage, the remedies, and the time frame for the Aratere resuming
service. A Transport Accident Investigation Commission inquiry has also been opened.
The big hurdle to get over in an urgent de bate application is whether the matter has
reached the stage where the business of the House should be set aside. The test is a high
one. Every incident cannot be the basis for a debate, even though, on the face of it, the
incident may be significant. I am not convinced  that I would be justified in setting aside
the business of the House today. The application is therefore declined.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I move, That the
House take note of miscellaneous business . What we have is the “Yeah, Nah Labour
Party”. We have a wishy-washy party with a wishy-washy leader that does not know
what it stands for or what it really means. What we have is the “Yeah, Nah Labour
Party”. It cannot decide where it stands a nd cannot decide what it means. Labour wants
to be the “Assure Party”. What it is actua lly is the “Unsure Party”. Labour does not
know what it stands for. You have got to sa y that at least the Greens know what they
stand for, and that is agains t anything that will actually mean jobs and growth. David
6 Nov 2013 General Debate 14407
Shearer may have been the “Yeah, um” leader  but now we have the “Yeah, nah” leader.
There is no doubt about that.
Let us take the man ban—take the man ban as one example. Labour turned round and
said: “Yes, yes, we want a man ban. We want a man ban.”, and then: “No, no, no, yeah,
yeah, no, no, no, we don’t want a man ban.” Then, of course, we have just had the
weekend, when it came back again and sa id: “Yeah, yeah, yeah, we will.” So it is
“Yeah, nah, yeah.” We have got one for that.
Let us take Cunliffe, who does the “Yeah ” to one audience and then “Nah” to
another audience. Inside the New Zealand C ouncil of Trade Unions conference we had
“Yeah” to the living wage and “Yeah” to paid parental leave. Then, quite frankly, he
stepped outside and went: “Oh, nah. Oh, na h—yeah, nah. Yeah, nah. Yeah, we kind of
want them, but we’ll just back-pedal here fa ster than Shane Jones does with a remote.
Yeah, nah, we actually didn’t mean it, or maybe  at some stage if we can get to it.”
Cunliffe is telling one audience “Yeah”, but then again, he does owe the unions,
remember. So one message to the unions—in fa ct, David Cunliffe might be at the meat
workers’ union now instead of in Parliament , and showing that he actually owes it
something and that that is where he should be.
Labour’s position on big, big projects is: “Y eah, nah. Yeah, we sort of want jobs and
that rhetoric sounds good, so yeah, we’ll go on about jobs. But nah, nah, we won’t
actually support anything or vote for anything that means growth or that means jobs for
real families.” In fact, let us take the classic example of that, which is the New Zealand
International Convention Centre. It is the t opic of the week. Let us take the convention
centre. Labour said: “Yeah, nah, yeah, nah, we won’t be voting for the convention
centre. Yeah, nah, we don’t support jobs . We don’t want $400 million dollars that
taxpayers won’t have to pay. Yeah, nah, we don’t want more tourism. Yeah, nah, we
don’t want to see those jobs coming in.” Unless, of course, Labour is speaking to
Skycity itself, then it is: “Oh, yeah, yeah. Ac tually, if we’re in, we won’t roll back the
contract. Actually, if we’re in, the word on this side is yeah, nah.”

items.speaker: Cunliffe says
items.text: “We didn’t mean what we actually said.” Let us just quote from him
here, when he said to Skycity: “Do you want it straight from the shoulder? Here it is.
We will not rip up the contract. We will not throw out the terms of Skycity’s gaming
licence.”—yeah, nah. Yeah, nah.
His rhetoric this week, the “Yeah, no” on what he is doing—in one breath on that
convention centre he has most certainly done the “Yeah, nah”. His response to the
unions right now—and let us remember who he is responsible to. Le t us take trade.
Trade is a goody, is it not? When he was in  Government, he said: “Oh, yeah, we need
more trade. Yeah, we’ll support trade. Free trade is good for the c ountry. Free trade is
good for jobs for Kiwis.” But now that the unions have got him wrapped round their
little finger, it is: “Nah, nah—well, maybe. Yeah, nah, yeah, nah, maybe we’ll support
free trade. No, we don’t think we will now.” because the unions are actually pulling the
strings, not the “Yeah, nah” leader who, quite frankly, is so wishy-washy.

items.speaker: Let us take superannuation. David Cunliffe  says
items.text: “Yeah, we want people to work
harder. Yeah, we want people to work longer. Nah, nah, not now the unions are actually
running things. Nah, it doesn’t s it quite as well, so we’ll just backtrack hugely on that
one as well.”, as he is kind of moving along.
Take national standards. In 2012—just last  year—we had it quite  emphatically from
the Labour Party: “No, we will not cancel na tional standards.” Now that the unions are
pulling the strings, it is: “Yeah, nah. Yeah, na h.” Just last weekend we had the leader
saying that he would scrap na tional standards: “Yeah, nah. Yeah, nah. We’re not really
sure exactly where we stand on those things as well.”
14408 General Debate 6 Nov 2013
So, let us contrast that to the National Pa rty, which stands for something. What will
the public be saying next year to Labour? “Yeah, nah.”

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I move for an extension of time. The more the public hear of this, the better for
us.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Stop the press. Stop the press.
We have just seen and heard the New Z ealand parliamentary equivalent of that
European zoo news story—the cross between the zebra and the donkey.
They are worried. They are worried on the other side of this House. They are
worried. We see it in their faces. They know it in National. Labour is on the move. We
are energised. We are confident. We ar e cohesive. We are buoyed by a fantastic
conference. The media caught the mood. Th e media got it. Vernon Small from the
Fairfax Group said that David Cunliffe “h it all the right notes … a new state-owned
insurer to appeal nationally  as well as to earthquake -weary premium-payers in
Christchurch, and a flawless delivery.” In the New Zealand Herald John Armstrong said
that David Cunliffe’s conference speech was “a  tour de force in terms of tone, content
and delivery.” Thank you, David. What a conf erence. David Cunliffe successfully laid
out his and Labour’s vision for New Zealand: to build a future for all, an economy that
works for all New Zealanders, a fair and just society where all live in dignity, an
environment we protect, and a nation we can be proud of.
All the while, National is increasingly out  of touch and failing New Zealanders.
There is a two-speed economy where many, esp ecially in the regions, are left behind;
widening inequality; an incompetent, anti-democratic Gove rnment; and crony
capitalism with corporate welf are for the connected few at the expense of the people.
National is so flat. This week it is mired in yet another controversy born of Steven
Joyce’s incompetence. This time it is Chor us and ultra-fast broadband—“Mr Fix-it”
now spelt that other way. It is yet anothe r instance of economi c mismanagement by
National. John Key’s respons e is to undermine the regu lator and consider more
corporate welfare.
Labour is on the move. As John Armstrong said, “The buzzword of the conference
was ‘energised’,”, and he is right. Alrea dy, many polls show La bour and our potential
MMP coalition partners ahead of National an d its shabby, discredited allies, ACT,
whose John Banks is in the dock for electo ral fraud, and Peter D unne, who, having lost
his party, was dumped for leaking a Government report.
We announced a significant move to us e the successful Kiwibank model for
insurance. I have not got time to dwell on that, but suffice it to say how shrill Mr Joyce
was when he was sent out to head the spi n. And how dumb of Mr English to call the
idea dumb, insulting hundreds of thousands of  New Zealanders, his former president
Ross Armstrong, and editorial writers across the country.
I want to end on Canterbury housing. Given the abject failure of National on housing
in Auckland, I should not have been surpri sed to find how incompetent its efforts in
Christchurch have been. But I really was surprised because at one level what we
announced was so simple. The “Human Wrecking Ball” is so blunt. He is great at
demolition, but he lacks the subtlety to govern, to stop the waste of short-term rentals,
and to give building affordable housing a boost in the devastated suburbs in
Christchurch East. We caught National flat -footed, and it was so easy because it is
ideologically opposed to doing this sort of thing.
On the front page of the Press—two-thirds of the front page—the banner headline
was “New era for New Brighton?”. It is ab out practical help for Christchurch in
partnership with the council.  And how did Nick Smith and Gerry Brownlee both miss
6 Nov 2013 General Debate 14409
it? It is so obvious. It is because they are so ideologically opposed to affordable
housing. They cannot blame the Resource Mana gement Act this time because it is
already in the Christchurch plan. It is already there; they just did not find it.
KiwiBuild will deliver it. This is how good Governments govern. We use the power
of the State to make a difference. We caught  the National Government flat-footed. Nick
Smith’s lame response in the Press on Monday was: “The Government has also made
early steps to investigate affordable housing areas in the city.” Fi ve years after being
elected and 3 years after the quake, National has been caught not just flat-footed and not
just stumbling but plain lame—lame.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Labour is not on the
move. I will tell you what: Labour is so disa ppointed with those figures that are out
today. It is so depressed about  those figures out today becau se the economy is growing.
Those figures out today prove it. The Oppos ition finance spokesperson, David Parker,
knows that the economy is moving and une mployment is on its way down, from 6.4
percent to 6.2 percent. That is fantastic when you consider all of the issues that this
Government has had to deal with. The une mployment rate was 7.2 percent a year ago.
Our policies are making a difference. Our po licies are really ge tting cut-through. Of
course when you consider that our economy is growing by 2.5 percent and then you
have a bank like Westpac out there forecasti ng 4 percent next year, it is no wonder that
the Labour Party is depressed.
For Mr Parker to get up here and say that Labour is on the move from its
conference—I cannot believe it. The only thing that I h eard that came out of its
conference was the man ban. The only thing that  came out was that it is back talking
about the man ban again, and half of the ma le members in the Labour caucus are really
worried about that.
Of course, the business confidence, which Mr Parker did not want to talk about, is at
an all-time high over the last 14 years. He forgot to mention that. Those members on the
other side of the House do not trust business, but over here we do. The business
confidence surveys are backing this Government.
What I want to also address this afternoon is the importance of regional infrastructure
and investment, the importance of innovation, and how we are going to continue to
grow our exports. Importantly, when you thi nk about the Opposition, and I thought this
article in the New Zealand Herald  recently summed it up really well, you have Russel
Norman over there objecting to pretty much  everything—in fact, he did. He objected to
everything: the Trans-Pacific Partnership,  Skycity, the Ruataniwha Water Storage
project, deep-sea oil exploration, the Denniston mine, the Pūhoi to Wellsford motorway,
saying Steven Joyce is agreeing with everyt hing and then saying on the monorail that
the Minister of Conservation still has to decide on that one—the list goes on.
Then you had Mr Cunliffe in the middle,  where he could not decide anything—
weasel words. Paula Bennett is exactly right : “Yeah, nah, yeah, nah, we are not really
sure.”
Let us think about the project just up the road from me, Transmission Gully. Labour
is not quite sure whether it s hould back that or not. Then you move up into my neck of
the woods, the Kapiti Expressway, and Labour is opposed to that. How are we going to
get the region of Manawat ū-Whanganui, which needs a bit of a kick-start, moving up?
We are going to need to invest in decent infrastructure. But our opponents over there are
against the 1,000 jobs to be created in my el ectorate when the road is built. They are
against it.
Then you move on to water storage projects. We know that the Greens over there are
against it. We could tell from their questio ning today from Russel Norman. Then you
get into the “Yeah, nah. ” over on the other side. They ar e not quite sure. On one hand,
14410 General Debate 6 Nov 2013
you have got David Cunliffe saying “Yea h, nah.”, but then you have Ruth Dyson
recently in the paper talking about the Ru ataniwha Water Storage project, where she
said that the Government woul d be irresponsible to proceed with this scheme. So once
again, “Yeah, nah.” They are not really sure  about investing in the regional economy.
They are not sure about the $4 billion of exports that decent water storage and irrigation
projects would create.
The other thing that is  really important is investing in innovation. We need to invest
in innovation. That is why we are investing in the Primary Growth Partnership. It is a
very, very successful innovation project.  There are 16 projects and $684 million
invested by industry and backed by the Government. You had David Shearer, when he
was the leader, out there sayi ng that increasing spending on innovation is a crucial step
for the New Zealand economy. So on that si de of the House you should have them
supporting the Primary Growth Partnership, but they want to attack it negatively. They
want to attack investment in our primary i ndustries. I cannot believe it. They should be
out there supporting it.
Then we move into trade. Then we move  into trade. Phil Goff knows the importance
of the Trans-Pacific Partnership. Phil Goff should stand up in his call this afternoon and
say that Labour is going to back and s upport the Trans-Pacific Partnership. Will Mr
Goff say that this afternoon? Well, we look forwar d to Mr Goff standing up this
afternoon and saying that Labour is going to back the Trans-Pacific Partnership, worth
$2 billion in exports. I bet he does not.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: It is a good place to
start—will Labour members stand up and say they will support the Trans-Pacific
Partnership? “Yeah, nah.” When they are talk ing to the farmer audience they will say
yes; when they are talking to their union audience they will say na h. The one thing that
is interesting about that, which both of my colle agues left out, is that the best response
to Labour members is to say “Yeah, right!”.
Let us have a look at what Labour member s have said out in the provinces. They
have been up in Taranaki just recently. Th e soon-to-be new leader of the Labour Party,
the Hon Shane Jones, visited Taranaki and he said: “Loo k, we’re not frightening to
business. We’re not frightening to growth. We  like the primary industries. We like the
provinces, and we’re here to help.” Of course, he had in tow with him the once
wannabe, and long-since-disappeared, Andrew Little as a co-pilot.
Let us have a look at what Labour members said when they were in Taranaki: “We’ll
promote growth in the primary sector. We’ll promote growth in the development of the
province.” But the problem is, of course, that in provincial New Zealand we have seen a
maximum exodus to Australia, we have seen  a huge decline in economic growth, and
we have seen a massive loss of jobs. I t hought I had better go and research that, so I
went and got Venture Taranaki’s  latest paper, which it has just released. What does it
say? The rate of population growth is up, the economic outlook is up, employment
numbers are up, the employment participation rate is up, and the employment outlook is
up. But numbers are up in terms of the skills shortage. Well, that is a negative. Skills
shortages are up—there is something for Labour to hang on to.
The paper goes on to say that natural in creases in population are up, long-term
international arrivals are up, house valu es are up, house sales are up, values for
residential construction consen ts are up, and the number of  dairy cattle is up. Labour
members will probably see that as a negative. They will probably see more dairy cattle
as a negative. The number of farms for sale  is up, port activity is  up, and the number of
18-year-olds with National Certificate of E ducations Achievement level 2 or equivalent
is up.
6 Nov 2013 General Debate 14411
Something seems to be wrong with the “Yeah, nah—yeah, right!” approach here
because the story Labour is putting forward is quite different compared with the facts.
In fact, just recently we saw that Taranaki was leading in all of the statistics: economic
growth, the average wage, and in terms of  opportunity going forward. The question,
then, is why. Well, here we go. Once again, Labour members have said that they will be
totally supportive of the primary sector. Well, in Taranaki—and it will come as a
surprise to Labour members—we have the da iry industry. On the one hand they say:
“Yes, that’s a good thing, and we should encour age it.”, but on the other hand they will
say: “Well, actually, we’re too dependent on it.” Well, there is another industry in the

items.speaker: Taranaki as well
items.text: the energy industry. On the one hand they say that it is wonderful, but
on the other hand they say: “We’ve got to be careful with where we go looking for oil
and drilling for oil.”
But there is a third industry, and it was onc e as big, and that is  the meat and wool
sector. Labour members know that internationally New Zealand lamb already has a very
high brand value. You can go to supermarkets or restaurants anywhere in the world and
be told that New Zealand lamb is a very sought-after product. We know that
internationally it is fetching about half the pr ice it could. So what is Labour’s response
to that? That is the first question I would ask. What is its policy on that?
I look forward to hearing from Labour memb ers, because if they are concerned that
the dairy industry is too dominant in the economic drivers of the New Zealand
economy, why not lift some of the others? Why not bring some of the others up to the
dairy industry’s level? I thi nk that probably Sir Ralph Norri s’s response in the recent
report on the Fonterra scare sums it up perfectly. He said: “New Zealand society is often
described as egalitarian. It has never had a European style in herited aristocracy.” As the
son of a sharemilker, I am very pleased abou t that. But the problem with that is that
Labour will not support winners. It is ca lled the tall poppy syndrome, the “Yeah, nah
syndrome”, or, if you like, the “Yeah, right!” syndrome. Economic growth from Labour
is, I think, summed up perfectly by saying “Yeah, right!”.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: It has been very rare for me to follow
two positive speeches—one by the Hon Nathan Guy and the other by Shane Ardern—
talking about positive things. It is my pleasure to participate in the general debate today.
We have been celebrating Diwa li in our Parliament since 2005. As we celebrate Diwali
today in Parliament once again, I feel proud to reside in a country that values all cultural
diversity. May I also share that we are a sm all nation. However, we  have close to 100
nationalities living in this beau tiful country. The reason for th is, of course, is the very
welcoming and open attitude of New Zealande rs. All migrants play a very important
role in building trad e and cultural ties between their na tive countries and their adopted
country, which is New Zealand.
I would also like to take th is opportunity to congratulate  the Indian Space Research
Organisation on the successful launch of the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, flight C25,
into Mars’ orbit. With this  successful launch, India ha s entered a group of select
countries, with its first Mars mission announced as a success.
In the past month or so I have had the opportunity to travel across New Zealand to
attend Diwali celebrations. It was wonderful to see that in most of the places I visited
the majority of people attending Diwali celebrations were not of Indian origin; rather,
these were New Zealanders who have embr aced and open-heartedly accepted Indian
Kiwis. I could see people enjoying the food, the dances, and the cultural performances,
and buying ethnic dresses for themselves and their children.
Another wonderful example of New Zeal anders having positively embraced Indian
Kiwis is in our sports teams.  Ish Sodhi, a Kiwi Indian cric keter, was recently included
in the Black Caps squad and represented the New Zealand cricket team against
14412 General Debate 6 Nov 2013
Bangladesh. Before Ish, we had Dipak Patel an d Jeetan Patel, both cricketers of Indian
Kiwi origin who represented New Zealand. It is my drea m to see a person of Asian
ethnicity make it into the mighty All Blacks one day.
Ethnic communities have educated us about  new ways of living and doing things.
These may not necessarily be what we are us ed to. It is the difference of other eating
patterns, lifestyles, and social behaviour, and it gives New Zealand its international
flavour. This is a very positive lesson that I learnt long ago. It is not right. It is not
wrong. It is just different. I choose to live and learn from this statement.
The Christchurch earthquake  was no doubt a tragic and un forgettable event in the
history of this country. However, the be st thing for me to see each time I visit
Christchurch is how different cultures and communities help each other and continue to
do so without any prejudice. As I visit different parts of New Zealand, I continue to hear
great things that New Zealanders share with me on the work of this National
Government. While the Opposition continues with negativity, the growing reality is that
the average New Zealander is positive about the direction that the leader of the National
Party, the Rt Hon John Key, is taking us in. Ordinary New Zealanders are very happy
with the progress we have made. When the rest  of the world lags at subzero levels of
growth, we manage to average about 2 percent.
The recent survey by the Bank of New Zeala nd reveals that business confidence at
present is at the highest level in decades . There are no doubts in my mind that the
migrant community of New Zealand has co ntributed to our nation’s growth and
business confidence. The recent media releas e by Statistics New Zealand confirms that
employment growth continues in the labour market. The employment rate rose to 64.4
percent, and unemployment fell to 6.2 per cent. Over the September 2013 quarter the
number of people employed rose by 2.4 percent in the household labour force survey.
Demand for workers from established busines ses rose by 1.9 percent in the quarterly
employment survey.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: And now back to the future. I have spent
a bit of time in Canterbury lately, and I am convinced that one of the great failings of
this Government is the Canterbury rebuild. It has been a case of too slow, too little, and
woefully lacking in execution. It has been  3 years since the first Christchurch
earthquake—3 years—and the rebuild is onl y just beginning. Th at is unbelievable.
Three years of waiting. The people of Canterbu ry have just endured  their third winter
since the earthquakes, and too many people in Canterbury are putting up with a housing
crisis that has seen them paying hundreds of do llars every week to rent a caravan or to
squash a family into a sleepout or someone’s spare room. It is totally unacceptable.
Rents are up 25 percent in Canterbury since December 2011. House prices are the
highest and the most unaffordable in any city outside Auckland. The Government’s own
officials say that up to 7,400 people in Canter bury are officially homeless. Nick Smith
and then Gerry Brownlee today got up in th is House and said that there is no housing
crisis in Canterbury; there is just a challenge. Well, the challenge is for the people of
Canterbury putting up with a Government th at has demonstrated two massive blind
spots when it comes to the Canterbury rebuild.
The first blind spot has been Gerry Brow nlee and Nick Smith’s oversight, if you
could call it that. It might be that affordable  housing is a technicality for National. It
might be that it is a minor matter for Nati onal, but the Government has completely
overlooked affordability when it comes to th e rebuild. There are houses being built on
the outskirts of the city, on new greenfields land, in developments like Wigram Skies
and Prestons Road, but few, if any, of them  are affordable for ordinary Cantabrians.
This is a huge gap in the re build, and Labour will plug that  gap. We will deliver 10,000
6 Nov 2013 General Debate 14413
affordable starter homes for first-home buyers over 4 years—high-quality, affordable
homes for first-home buyers.
The other big blind spot of this Government’s approach to the rebuild is that it is a lot
better at demolition than it is at building. The “Human Wrecking Ball”, Gerry
Brownlee, gave himself wartime powers to co mpulsorily acquire new land. He has used
those powers mostly to demolish, not to build. The great Lyndon Johnson once said that
any jackass can kick down a barn, but it take s a craftsman to build one. That says it all
about Gerry Brownlee’s approach to the Chri stchurch rebuild. This is why the rebuild
has been so slow—Gerry Brownlee thinks that demolition and hope is a rebuild plan.
That is why Labour has announced the form ation of the New Brighton Community
Revitalisation Project. We will back the effo rts of local residents in New Brighton. We
will back the local business community. We  will work with the council. We will
consolidate the old retail ar ea in New Brighton, which has fallen on hard times, and we
will turn that community into a vibrant,  modern, character beachside suburb, with
hundreds of new units of affordable housing.
New Brighton is a microcosm of many other parts of Canterbury. It is a community
that has been knocked around by the earthquak es. It has fantastic natural assets,
including an amazing beach. It is close to the Avon- Ōtākaro river precinct. What is
missing is a Government prepared  to roll up its sleeves and b ack the efforts of the local
community. I cannot believe th at this National Government  has missed New Brighton
as an opportunity to revitalise that commun ity and help rebuild the kind of place where
Cantabrians want to live, to work, and to play.
Labour’s approach is creative. It is  hands-on. We announced a package of
announcements on the weekend, including Kiwi Assure and including the smart use of
empty but habitable houses in the red z one. We promised 10,000 affordable starter
homes in Canterbury over 10 years, and we will get behind the efforts of local people in
New Brighton. We will work with the Christ church City Council, with the private
sector, and with the community to revitalise New Brighton. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: I first want to pay my respects and condolences to
Lotu-Iiga Lotuatamaiti, Sam Lotu-Iiga’s fa ther, who passed away suddenly this week,
and also to Peter Fatialofa, the former capta in of Manu Samoa. They were two sons of
Samoa, so my condolences go to both families.
Twenty years ago today—it sounds like a song—on 6 November 1993, I entered this
House. Today is the 20 th anniversary of that. I want to thank first of all the Rt Hon
Winston Peters of New Zealand First for gi ving me my shot at politics. And no, it was
not my second party: it was my first.
I have been in for 6 years, I was out for 6 years, and I have been in for 8 years. I
know it sounds like a lag and I know it sounds like a prison  sentence—a prison term—
but in 20 years, I have seen them come a nd I have seen them go. I have seen changes
and I have seen things that stay the same. Th ere has been one constant in all of those 20
years: Labour has no idea. It never did have an idea, and it never will have an idea. Just
imagine if it ever got the reins of power to dr ive the ship. If it was a captain of a ship, it
would spend like a drunken sailor.
But that is not all. See, th ere is nothing wrong with spendi ng like a drunken sailor if
it is your own money. But the fact of the matter remains that when you spend like a
drunken sailor and it is not your money, it is the taxpayers’ money, and then there is
something seriously wrong. It was pork barrel politics then and it is pork barrel politics
now.
Before he went away, Mr Tw yford got up in this House and he said: “In the great
words of Lyndon Baines Johnson”—I could not believe my luck. There was the biggest
racist bigot from Texas that the United Stat es has ever known. In fact, what he did was
14414 General Debate 6 Nov 2013
to send the world into the Viet Nam War, and this from Phil Twyford, the member of
Parliament in my own area. I am shocked and I am horrified. The message to children
out there is when you go home tonight, read  about who Lyndon Baines Johnson really
was. He was the one who sent people to the Viet Nam War. He was the one who—oh,
so this is the great Lyndon Baines Johnson. Therein lies the answer to the question. Can
these guys deliver? Can these guys run the ship? Absolutely not . And you know why?
Do you know why? Because they rely on old, outdated models like Lyndon Baines
Johnson for their thinking. That is where the thinking of Mr Twyford comes from.
Look, I do not know. Let us take Skycity. Labou r railed against the Skycity deal, but
on the other hand took tickets from Skycity to go to the rugby. Let us take a look at the
man ban. It does not know whether it is Ar thur or Martha. For goodness’ sake! Labour
wants it both ways—50c here and 50c ther e. Do you know why? Because it does not
have an idea. It never had an idea. In fact , what it is doing is apologising for stuff it did
20-odd years ago. But really—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: They want to do it again.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Labour wants to do it again. So what it is going to do is have
KiwiAssure. It will get this thing up and r unning, and then what is the bet that it will
sell it? For goodness’ sake! For goodness’ sake. We have been there, we have done that,
we have bought the T-shirt, and we ain’t voting Labour again.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Can I begin by congratulating you, Mr
Speaker, on your New York City Marathon ru n and by saying that it is an excellent
example to the rest of the House. I want to  acknowledge Tau Henare and all the rest of
the 1993 intake for their 20-year anniversary today. It feels like just  the other day that
Tau and I were newbies in this House. I have stayed with the same party, actually, while
I have been in the House because I backed a winner to start with. I did not need to
change parties to stay in Parliament, but  I still acknowledge the 20-year contribution
that Tau and others have made.
I want to congratulate the Labour Party on showing its support for Canterbury by
having its annual conference in Christchurch. When it was first suggested, those of us
from Canterbury took a bit of a deep breath and said: “Woah!  This is a big ask. How is
Canterbury going to cope with this? How w ill the Christchurch Labour team handle
that?”. Of course, we were worried, frankl y, that not a lot of people would come to
Canterbury. It is a lot easier for the majo rity of the populati on who live north of
Hamilton to go to a conference in Auckland. We were overwhelmed by the number of
delegates who came to our city. People came because they wanted to support
Canterbury, but, actually, I think there was a nother side. They came because they knew
that this was going to be a weekend of exciting debate, of fresh ideas, and of a clear
vision for an alternative to the current Government.
We want a Government that is in touch with people and that understands the needs
and aspirations of, and the future chances  for, New Zealanders, and we want a
Government that will give every New Zealander a stake in that future. That is what
Labour talked about on the weekend, and that is  what we want to deliver next year. The
whole conference was so energising. We ha d some great debates. We always do. The
media were not up to the bigger-picture issues . They just shared the more contentious, I
suppose, issues with people, but I know that the debates on the floor of our conference
were challenging and exciting.
It does put Labour in stark co ntrast with the cu rrent Government. We have seen so
many examples of the out-of-touch and, fra nkly, arrogant performance of the John Key
- led Government that people, particular ly in Canterbury but, I know, all over the
country, are really asking: “What does it take to make this Government connect with the
people? What does it take to make it listen to the people? What does it take to make it
6 Nov 2013 General Debate 14415
understand?”. A recent example is Gerry Brownl ee, with a very, very harsh report from
the Auditor-General about the performa nce of the Earthquake Commission in
Canterbury, and Gerry Brownl ee brushes it off. He says: “Oh, everyone seems pretty
happy.” Well, he may not have been outside  his own home in Christchurch, because
people are not happy with the performance of the Earthquake Commission, and they are
not happy with the performance of insurance companies. People are feeling threatened
and bullied. They are being given low-ball offers, and they feel as if they have very little
alternative. They are feeling powerless against the weight of insurance companies.
That is why people in our city were so excited at Labour’s proposal to have
KiwiAssure, an insurance company that puts people first, that is service-focused, and
that says: “Our customers are the most importa nt part of our business.” That is what we
want in Canterbury. We are fed up with insu rance companies that forget that we have
paid premiums to them for years for cover. When we need that response from them, we
expect to get what we paid for. That is not what many people are getting. We want to
make sure that the business of the insurance company is about the people and their
needs. We have heard the criticism from th e National Party and th e insurance industry,
just the same way as we heard that very sa me criticism from the National Party and the
banking sector when we proposed to intr oduce Kiwibank, and what a success that has
been. We need guarantees of security. We wa nt a business that invests in New Zealand
and New Zealanders first above profit. That is what KiwiAssure will do, in the same
way as Kiwibank has done.
National wants to sell off the profitable industries that New Zealanders have built up.
We want to invest in them for the future  of New Zealand and for the future of New
Zealanders. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: To evoke an old Spike Milligan song, Labour is
walking backwards for Christmas. And not only back for Christmas—right on back to
the 1970s. We are hearing alarming echoes of S oviet Union statist po licies in the form
of a State-run insurance company and a State-controlled electricity market. Free trade—
and we have got one of the proponents of it over there. I have got to pay credit to the
member Mr Phil Goff, who negotiated the free- trade agreement with China. Free trade
has long been a bipartisan agreement, but  now the current leader is questioning
Labour’s support for the Trans-Pacific Partne rship, while Labour’s ex-leader is saying
“Labour should continue to back it.” But what the leader, the dithering David Cunliffe,
is saying to one audience, he might not be saying to another audience. “Will we back it?
Well, maybe, yeah—nah, nah.”
Labour is painting a picture of itself as a party bemused, befuddled, bewildered, and
becalmed, and certainly as one that is unfit  to govern. With Labour at the helm, New
Zealand’s ship of State would veer danger ously on to the rocks of higher borrowing,
higher spending, and higher taxes—the very po licies that pushed New Zealand into the
global financial crisis 6 to 12 months before the rest of the world. A Labour
Government supported by the Greens would be an absolute disaster for New Zealand, in
stark contrast with the steady, considered , prudent financial management that has
characterised the National-led Government’s stewardship of the country’s finances over
the last 5 years. This pr incipled and pragmatic Government continues to work
relentlessly for the benefit of every New Z ealander, adjusting the mesh in many areas
and at a multitude of levels. It has succeeded in cushioning vulnerable New Zealanders
from the ongoing effects of the worst economic conditions in decades, and one only has
to look at the situation abroad to realise how fortunate we are in this country.
Over the years the Government’s prudent  financial management of the nation’s
finances has received ri nging endorsements from star s in the world economic
firmament. It has been noted that reduci ng our exposure to overseas debt markets as
14416 General Debate 6 Nov 2013
much as possible whilst, as I mentioned before, still cushioning vulnerable New
Zealanders from the harshest edges of the ongoing global financial crisis—we are doing
that. Our considered fiscal stewardshi p means that New Zealand’s economy is
performing better than the US, the UK, Ge rmany, the bulk of the eurozone, and, of
course, Japan. The effects of th e drought earlier in the year have largely been shrugged
off, and we are witnessing a continued uptur n in the non-agricultural sectors as well,
meaning that the New Zealand economy is set to go for a substantial acceleration of
growth in the second half of this year and beyond.
Growth is occurring, as we have heard, across a range of sect ors in addition to
construction and housing. Consumer spending is  growing at an incr easing space, with
spending on services particularly strong over the June quart er. Manufacturing and
services activities surveys have put in cons istently strong readings over this year.
China’s insatiable demand for our primary products means our export earnings are
looking very healthy.
It is gratifying that the e xpansion is becoming more cons istent across the region. My
colleague here mentioned Taranaki—many of  us call it “Taradise”—where the twin
pillars, the black and white  pillars, of oil and milk  are propping up the economy and
causing it to grow hugely. In fact, it is leading New Zealand as we speak.
This is a Government that is getting results for all New Zealanders. Our focus has
been on growth that is sustainable and bu ilt on higher savings and earnings, rather than
ever-more-increasing debt and greater cons umption. As I have noted previously, our
prudent policies have been  praised by Peter Orszag, President Obama’s previous
Director of the Office of Management and Budget. He praised New Zealand as standing
out in the world as the only country that ha s coupled additional economic stimulus with
medium-term fiscal consolidation. Not surp risingly, huge numbers of New Zealanders
report suffering nightmares at the thought of our  measured approach being replaced by
an economy measured by a coalition of money-printing Greens and a Labour Party
bereft of strong leadership, dithering and dodging and answerable only to its union
masters.
Other support of the Government’s economic management has come from the IMF’s
Managing Director, Christine Lagarde, who praised the Government’s economic policy
Business Growth Agenda, and described th e New Zealand economy as being very
